problem: Learning perception and sensorimotor control in the physical world is slow, costly and hard to scale. Existing simulators (SUNCG-based, game engines such as ViZDoom, Malmo, GTA5, THOR, CARLA) use synthetic scenes or weak rendering pipelines, so they oversimplify the visual world and leave a large sim-to-real perception gap.
motivation: Active agents need a steady stream of egocentric observations while they stay subject to physical constraints. Simulation is the practical way to provide this, but only if the simulated scenes are as semantically complex as real ones and the rendered images are close to what a real camera would capture. Scans of real buildings supply the semantic complexity for free. Paired rendered/real images then make it possible to learn a mapping that dissolves the remaining appearance gap in both directions.
key_idea: Build a simulator by virtualizing 572 scanned real buildings. Novel views are synthesized with point-cloud rendering plus a neural 'filler' network f, which is jointly trained with a backward network u ('Goggles') that maps real camera images into the rendering domain, so a policy trained on f(Is) can be deployed on u(It) without further domain adaptation.
insight: The mapping from renderings to real images is not bijective: there is no unique way to fill dis-occlusions, so refining renderings alone (S→T) cannot close the gap. Training f and u jointly so that f(Is)≈u(It), plus a term f(Is)≈It that prevents collapse, meets the two domains in the middle. The ablations make this clear. Neural refinement alone actually hurts transfer to raw real images: depth error rises from 1.026 (Is→It) to 1.560 (f(Is)→It), and policy logit discrepancy rises from 0.242 to 0.300. Adding Goggles gives the best results: depth error 0.915 (0.91 in Fig. 7a) against a real→real gold standard of 0.86, and policy discrepancy 0.204. Nearest-neighbour retrieval (top-1 91.6% for f(Is)→Is, 85.9% for u(It)→It) shows the two networks do not cheat by collapsing images.
method: Gibson space database: 572 full buildings, 1447 floors, 211k m² scanned with NavVis, Matterport and DotProduct devices. Each space has RGB-D panoramas with global poses and reconstructed meshes. 2D-3D-S and Matterport3D are also integrated.

Geometric point-cloud rendering: the k nearest RGB-D panoramas are reprojected to the target 6-DoF view. A depth test against the target-view depth (0.1 m threshold) filters out points that should be occluded. Points from all panoramas are merged by density-weighted soft selection, weight exp(λd·di)/Σm exp(λd·dm), and then bilinearly interpolated.

Neural filler f: an 18-layer dilated-conv CNN (3×3 kernels, max dilation 32; 48- or 256-kernel variants for speed vs. quality) that fixes artifacts and fills dis-occlusions. It uses a stochastic identity initialization (half the weights random and frozen, the rest optimized to reproduce the input).
Loss: VGG16 perceptual loss plus an L1 term that matches the mean colour of 32×32 tiles (colour-moment matching). This outperformed GAN losses.

Goggles u: a backward network with the same architecture that maps real images It toward renderings. It is trained jointly with L = E[D(f(Is),It)] + E[D(f(Is),u(It))] on 4.3k paired panoramas. At deployment it acts as the agent's corrective glasses.

Embodiment and physics: PyBullet with collision, gravity and Coulomb friction. Any URDF/MJCF agent can be imported (humanoid, ant, Husky, drone, Minitaur, JackRabbot). PID, nonholonomic and ideal positional controllers are provided, along with depth, normal, semantic and proprioceptive channels behind an OpenAI Gym interface.

setting.backbone: Simulator renderer: 18-layer dilated CNN filler f + Goggles u (same architecture), trained from scratch with stochastic identity init. Demo agents: PPO policies trained from scratch. Depth-estimation and scene-classification networks are unspecified.
setting.training_data: f/u: 4.3k paired 1024×2048 rendered/real panoramas, randomly cropped to 256×256 (50 epochs f alone, then 50 epochs joint; 3 days on 2 Titan X). Demo RL agents trained in Gibson with PPO: local planning 150 episodes / 150k frames; distant navigation emerges after 1700 episodes / 680k frames; stair descent after 1700 episodes / 700k steps.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB and/or depth (also normals and semantics available) plus 'non-visual sensory' input: agent position, orientation and relative position to target.
setting.action_space: Husky nav tasks: 4 discrete actions (forward/backward/left/right). Ant stair task: 8-D continuous joint torques.
setting.privileged: The non-visual sensory input includes agent position, orientation and relative target position, even though the distant-navigation task description says no external odometry or GPS is given.

numbers_note: This is a simulator/environment paper and reports no standard navigation benchmark (no SR/SPL). Results for the navigation demo tasks (local planning/obstacle avoidance, distant visual navigation) appear only as reward curves in Figs. 8–9. MMD/CORAL distances and the full 4×4 depth train/test matrix appear only in Fig. 7. The stair-climb result is given only as a relative figure ('outperformed the non-perceptual agent by 70%'). Train/test split sizes for the static transfer tasks are not stated, so 'test' and 'full' are nominal. Other own numbers in text: Table 1 Gibson database (572 spaces, 211k m², SSA 1.38, Nav. complexity 5.98, real-world transfer error 0.92); scene-diversity entropy 3.72; Table 2 rendering FPS; NN retrieval accuracies.
results: Joint training of the filler and Goggles gives the smallest sim-to-real gap. Training on f(Is) and testing on u(It) yields depth error 0.915 (0.91 in Fig. 7a, vs. 0.86 real→real gold standard), scene accuracy 0.291, SSIM 0.816, L1 0.051 and navigation-policy logit discrepancy 0.204, beating both the no-Goggles (f(Is)→It) and pre-network (Is→It) settings. At the database level, depth networks trained on Gibson transfer to real 2D-3D-S images with 0.92 m error, versus 2.89 for SUNCG and 2.11 for Matterport3D (both rendered with MINOS); Gibson's scene-class entropy is 3.72 vs. 2.89 (SUNCG) and 3.32 (THOR). Rendering runs faster than real time: 30.6 FPS RGBD at 256×256 with the full filler, 77.7 FPS at 128×128. In the demo tasks, only the visually-equipped agent solved distant navigation, and the perceptual ant generalized better on stairs, outperforming the non-perceptual agent by 70%.
limitations: No dynamic content (moving objects/people) and no manipulation support.
Scans lack material properties and physics simulation is imperfect, which may introduce physics-related domain gaps.

Goggles is validated mostly on static recognition tasks plus an offline policy-discrepancy check; there is no evaluation on a real robot. The navigation demos are only reward curves without standard metrics.
